To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the housing markets in London have amplified or entrenched labour-market differences.
the housing-market has amplified, or reinforced, the effects of labour-market differences on access to home ownership.
the gender gap in the take-up rate for home ownership in London has increased between 1971 and 1991, and that this gap has increased more rapidly in the more affluent areas of London.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which the housing market has been used to reproduce labour-market differences.
the ways in which the labour market, gender, and housing market are related.
the extent to which the housing market has contributed to the social polarisation of the city.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in general, professionalisation and feminisation are associated with a higher propensity to own a home in London, but this association is stronger in the high-status areas than it is in the low-status areas.
the housing market in London, and the wider UK, has been a major factor in the polarisation of society.

professionalisation and the feminisation of the labour force in London are associated with the polarisation of the housing market, with a tendency for the more advantaged to be able to move to more advantaged locations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the housing market is a major mechanism through which the occupational structure of London has been reproduced.
, in London, home ownership has become a class-based phenomenon and that the class-based nature of home ownership has become more entrenched in the 1980s than in the 1970s.
the housing market in London is increasingly polarised between a high-status and low-status housing market.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in London, the gendered nature of home-ownership has become more pronounced, and that this is associated with a process of sociospatial polarisation.
the housing market is not a level playing field.
the housing market is a mechanism for the reproduction of social inequalities.
